boor

BOOR (rhymes with 'tour') · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Boor is a rude, unrefined person who lacks social manners or sensitivity to others.

Everyone dreaded sitting near the office boor at the holiday lunch, since he always talked with his mouth full and interrupted every story.

Example

The tour group cringed when one member, a total boor, loudly complained about the local food in front of the restaurant's own staff.

A boor isn't just occasionally rude -- it's someone whose lack of social awareness makes them uncomfortable to be around in almost any polite setting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

oaf: An oaf is clumsy and slow-witted -- knocking over the punch bowl, missing the point of every joke. A boor may be perfectly coordinated and even clever; what a boor lacks is social grace, the sense of how to behave around other people.

philistine: A philistine is someone indifferent to art, culture, and refinement -- proud of never opening a book. A boor's failing is manners rather than taste: a boor can adore the opera and still talk through it with his mouth full.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gentleman: a polite, considerate man

sophisticate: a refined, socially polished person

Where it sits · how rough the bad manners get — tactless → boor → lout

tactless vs. boor: Tactless is milder than boor: a tactless person just blunders with an insensitive remark now and then, while a boor is unpleasant company across the board -- crude at the table, oblivious in conversation.

lout vs. boor: A lout (also in this unit) takes it even further than a boor, adding a rough, sometimes physically clumsy or threatening edge.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — boor

root — boor: peasant, farmer (extended to mean an unrefined person) (Middle Dutch/German boer)

Put it together

Put it together: Boor comes directly from the Dutch/German word boer, meaning 'farmer' or 'peasant.' Over time, English speakers used it dismissively to mean someone as coarse and unrefined as a country peasant was stereotyped to be -- which is exactly the insult behind boor today.

Use the root in a new word: Boer

Use the root in a new word: Boer: The Boers were Dutch-descended farmers who settled in South Africa -- their name comes from the very same root as boor, though 'Boer' itself carries no insult.

Word Building

Word Choice

Boor describes a specific kind of person -- someone whose lack of social grace makes them unpleasant company -- while its cousin lout (also in this unit) usually adds a rougher, sometimes physically oafish edge.
